doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Collingwood's Principles of Art at LSU: artist versus entertainer
summary: Allison credits an aesthetics course and Collingwood with his ideas on expression of emotion; Audre recalls the underlined book.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Well, here’s another quote, at the start of another chapter, about LSU. You say: “I tried to use the blues as a way of expressing myself. I had aesthetics in college, and before I began performing full-time, I already had an idea of how I wanted to approach my music. I picked up ideas from a philosophy of art course, such as the difference between the artist and the entertainer, and the difference between the betrayal of emotion and the expression of emotion. These influenced me.” At ths point, can you speak to the difference between the artist and the entertainer?
That’s all from a book, Collingwood...
Where is that Collingwood book? But you used to talk about it, what it meant to you.
The book was Principles of Art, by R.G. Collingwood, and it’s a book you immersed yourself in through an aesthetics course at LSU.
We still have that book, and it’s all underlined.
What did you say when you accepted that award at LSU? You said something about the influence it had on you.
Back Country Suite was all I remember from that... Mispronounced.
Oh, you mean somebody at that ceremony said “Black Country Suite” instead of “Back Country Suite.”
I’m just talking about what Collingwood said about art, what art is, kind of fired you up, that what you were doing was art.
I don’t know. I don’t remember...
You used to say something like “the honest expression...”
I haven’t thought about this in a long time.
